title: Best Indian Family Dramas
description: Families are Indian cinema's oldest subject. These are the films that got them right.
intro: A great Indian family drama gets the small rooms right before it tries anything grand.

entries.why_it_ranks: Four broken brothers slowly discovering affection, responsibility and what actually constitutes a family makes this one of modern Indian cinema's richest family dramas.
Amitabh Bachchan and Hema Malini turned the neglect of ageing parents into one of mainstream Hindi cinema's most emotionally powerful and widely discussed family stories.
A wonderfully observed multigenerational family drama where marriage, ego, money and generational differences collide inside an ordinary household.
Beneath the polished surface is an unusually honest portrait of resentment, secrets, parental favoritism and unresolved tensions inside a seemingly successful family.
Mohanlal anchors a devastating story of brotherhood, responsibility, guilt and the impossible emotional burden created by family tragedy.
Perhaps the definitive Indian celebration of the extended family, turning weddings, rituals, siblings and sacrifice into a cultural phenomenon.
A deeply affecting father-daughter story about education, money, dignity and a parent struggling to understand what his child actually needs.
The exhausting, funny and loving relationship between an ageing father and his independent daughter feels remarkably real.
A child returning to his ancestral home for a funeral observes the affection, tensions and secrets hidden inside an extended family.
A family revelation forces uncomfortable questions about marriage, fidelity, patriarchy and the different moral standards imposed on men and women.
Beneath the thriller machinery is an extraordinarily strong family story about how far an ordinary father will go to protect his wife and daughters.
Shekhar Kapur explores infidelity and parenthood through the devastating arrival of a child whose existence threatens an otherwise loving family.
Prakash Raj beautifully portrays a father discovering that loving his daughter also means learning to let her make a life beyond him.
A death brings an extended rural family together and gradually exposes grudges, pride, affection and relationships that have fractured over time.
A young man's relationship with his grandfather changes his understanding of career, food, responsibility and what a meaningful life looks like.
Sridevi's journey toward self-respect quietly exposes how easily a family can take a mother's labour, intelligence and dignity for granted.
Excessive and melodramatic, certainly — but few Indian films have turned parent-child conflict, adoption, separation and reunion into such enormous popular family spectacle.
A son searching for his father with Alzheimer's gradually confronts how little attention he had given the relationship while there was still time.
Almost entirely centred on an elderly couple, the film finds humour, companionship and tenderness in ordinary married life after the children have moved away.
A domestic worker's determination to educate her daughter creates a warm but honest examination of parental ambition, poverty and generational aspiration.
Mothers, daughters, neighbours and unconventional relationships form a warm portrait of contemporary urban family life.
Nana Patekar gives a towering performance as an ageing theatre legend confronting family estrangement, pride and the loss of everything that once defined him.
Domestic routine becomes a devastating examination of how supposedly normal family structures can conceal unequal expectations and unpaid labour.
Beneath the romance is an excellent father-son conflict about a loving parent whose constant control prevents his adult child from developing an independent identity.
An unexpected pregnancy in a middle-aged couple forces their adult children and extended family to confront embarrassment, intimacy, age and their own hypocrisy.
